claim: Defective mismatch repair leads to increased mutation rates.
source: Defective mismatch repair leads to increased mutation rates, and germline loss-of-function variants in the repair component MLH1 cause the hereditary cancer predisposition disorder known as Lynch syndrome.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of DNA repair and cancer biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Germline loss-of-function variants in MLH1 cause Lynch syndrome.
source: Defective mismatch repair leads to increased mutation rates, and germline loss-of-function variants in the repair component MLH1 cause the hereditary cancer predisposition disorder known as Lynch syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A majority of the disease-linked MLH1 variants studied are present at reduced cellular levels.
source: Here we show that a majority of the disease-linked MLH1 variants we studied are present at reduced cellular levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of steady-state levels of 69 MLH1 variants shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Destabilized MLH1 variants are targeted for chaperone-assisted proteasomal degradation.
source: We show that destabilized MLH1 variants are targeted for chaperone-assisted proteasomal degradation, resulting also in degradation of co-factors PMS1 and PMS2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased HSP70 binding (Figure 5A-B), proteasome inhibitor effects (Figure 3E), and cycloheximide chase experiments (Figure 3C-D).

claim: Degradation of destabilized MLH1 variants results in degradation of co-factors PMS1 and PMS2.
source: We show that destabilized MLH1 variants are targeted for chaperone-assisted proteasomal degradation, resulting also in degradation of co-factors PMS1 and PMS2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that PMS1 and PMS2 levels correlate with MLH1 levels (Figure 4).

claim: There is a correlation between structural destabilization, reduced steady-state levels and loss-of-function of MLH1 variants.
source: In silico saturation mutagenesis and computational predictions of thermodynamic stability of MLH1 missense variants revealed a correlation between structural destabilization, reduced steady-state levels and loss-of-function.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B-D comparing predicted ΔΔG values with measured steady-state levels and functional DME scores.

claim: Loss of stability and cellular degradation is an important mechanism underlying many MLH1 variants in Lynch syndrome.
source: Thus, we suggest that loss of stability and cellular degradation is an important mechanism underlying many MLH1 variants in Lynch syndrome.
evidence: This is based on the correlation between predicted stability, measured cellular levels, and pathogenicity shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Thermodynamic stability predictions combined with conservation analyses can separate disease-linked from benign MLH1 variants.
source: Combined with analyses of conservation, the thermodynamic stability predictions separate disease-linked from benign MLH1 variants, and therefore hold potential for Lynch syndrome diagnostics.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F demonstrating AUC of 0.90 for the logistic regression model combining FoldX and evolutionary sequence energies.

claim: The MutSα (MSH2-MSH6) heterodimer initiates mismatch repair by detecting the mismatch.
source: The MutSα (MSH2-MSH6) heterodimer initiates repair by detecting the mismatch after which the MutLα (MLH1-PMS2) heterodimer promotes the process by generating a nick in the newly synthesized DNA strand, thereby stimulating downstream repair proteins (Jiricny, 2006; Jun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiricny, 2006 and Jun et al., 2006.

claim: The MutLα (MLH1-PMS2) heterodimer promotes mismatch repair by generating a nick in the newly synthesized DNA strand.
source: The MutSα (MSH2-MSH6) heterodimer initiates repair by detecting the mismatch after which the MutLα (MLH1-PMS2) heterodimer promotes the process by generating a nick in the newly synthesized DNA strand, thereby stimulating downstream repair proteins (Jiricny, 2006; Jun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiricny, 2006 and Jun et al., 2006.

claim: The MMR pathway is phylogenetically highly conserved.
source: The MMR pathway is phylogenetically highly conserved, emphasizing its importance as a key DNA repair mechanism of the cell (Jiricny, 2013; Sachadyn, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiricny, 2013 and Sachadyn, 2010.

claim: Loss of MMR activity causes genome instability.
source: Loss of MMR activity causes genome instability, and can result in both sporadic and inherited cancer, such as Lynch syndrome (LS) (OMIM: #609310), also known as hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of DNA repair and cancer biology.

claim: Lynch syndrome is the underlying reason for around 4% of all colorectal cancer cases.
source: The predominant consequence of LS is colorectal cancer (CRC), making LS the underlying reason for around 4% of all CRC cases (Aarnio et al., 1999; Hampel et al., 2008; Sijmons and Hofstra, 2016; Vasen et al., 1996; Vasen and de Vos Tot Nederveen Cappel, 2013; Thompson et al., 2014; Møller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Aarnio et al., 1999; Hampel et al., 2008; and others.

claim: The cumulative lifetime cancer risk in Lynch syndrome patients varies considerably and depends on the specific germline mutation.
source: Importantly, the cumulative lifetime cancer risk varies considerably between patients and depends on the specific germline mutation in the genes encoding the key mismatch repair proteins MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2 (Barrow et al., 2008; Dowty et al., 2013; Dunlop et al., 1997; Lynch et al., 2015; Peltomäki et al., 1993; Plaschke et al., 2004; Sijmons and Hofstra, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Barrow et al., 2008; Dowty et al., 2013; and others.

claim: The majority of Lynch syndrome cases result from MLH1 and MSH2 mutations.
source: The majority of LS cases result from MLH1 and MSH2 mutations (Peltomäki, 2016), many of which are missense mutations (Heinen, 2010; Palomaki et al., 2009; Peltomäki and Vasen, 1997; Peltomäki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peltomäki, 2016 and others.

claim: Many Lynch syndrome-causing mutations in MLH1 and MSH2 are missense mutations.
source: The majority of LS cases result from MLH1 and MSH2 mutations (Peltomäki, 2016), many of which are missense mutations (Heinen, 2010; Palomaki et al., 2009; Peltomäki and Vasen, 1997; Peltomäki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heinen, 2010; Palomaki et al., 2009; and others.

claim: Missense mutations may cause loss-of-function by directly perturbing protein-protein interactions or ablating enzymatic activity.
source: Evidently, such missense mutations may cause loss-of-function by directly perturbing protein-protein interactions or ablating enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of how missense mutations can affect protein function.

claim: Many missense mutations cause loss-of-function by inducing structural destabilization of the protein.
source: Many missense mutations, however, cause loss-of-function by inducing structural destabilization of the protein (Stein et al., 2019), which in turn may trigger protein misfolding and degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) (Kampmeyer et al., 2017; Nielsen et al., 2014; Kriegenburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stein et al., 2019; Kampmeyer et al., 2017; Nielsen et al., 2014; and Kriegenburg et al., 2014.

claim: Structural destabilization may trigger protein misfolding and degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Many missense mutations, however, cause loss-of-function by inducing structural destabilization of the protein (Stein et al., 2019), which in turn may trigger protein misfolding and degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) (Kampmeyer et al., 2017; Nielsen et al., 2014; Kriegenburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kampmeyer et al., 2017; Nielsen et al., 2014; and Kriegenburg et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced cellular amount of a missense protein can ultimately cause disease.
source: As a result, the cellular amount of a missense protein may be reduced to an insufficient level, which can ultimately cause disease (Ahner et al., 2007; Casadio et al., 2011; Matreyek et al., 2018; Nielsen et al., 2017), as we and others have previously shown for LS-linked variants of MSH2 (Gammie et al., 2007; Arlow et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahner et al., 2007; Casadio et al., 2011; Matreyek et al., 2018; and Nielsen et al., 2017.

claim: Lynch syndrome-linked variants of MSH2 are degraded due to destabilization.
source: As a result, the cellular amount of a missense protein may be reduced to an insufficient level, which can ultimately cause disease (Ahner et al., 2007; Casadio et al., 2011; Matreyek et al., 2018; Nielsen et al., 2017), as we and others have previously shown for LS-linked variants of MSH2 (Gammie et al., 2007; Arlow et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gammie et al., 2007; Arlow et al., 2013; and Nielsen et al., 2017.

claim: Cellular abundance was determined for 69 MLH1 missense variants.
source: We determined cellular abundance for 69 missense variants, and show that several destabilized LS-linked MLH1 variants are targeted for chaperone-assisted proteasomal degradation and are therefore present at reduced cellular amounts.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Lower amounts of MLH1 result in degradation of MLH1-binding proteins PMS1 and PMS2.
source: In turn, this lower amount of MLH1 results in degradation of the MLH1-binding proteins PMS1 and PMS2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In silico saturation mutagenesis was performed for all possible MLH1 single site missense variants.
source: In silico saturation mutagenesis and computational prediction of the thermodynamic stability of all possible MLH1 single site missense variants revealed a correlation between the structural destabilization of MLH1, reduced steady-state levels and the loss-of-function phenotype.
evidence: This is described in the Methods section and results are shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Thermodynamic stability predictions accurately separate disease-linked MLH1 missense mutations from benign MLH1 variants with an AUC of 0.82.
source: Accordingly, the thermodynamic stability predictions accurately separate disease-linked MLH1 missense mutations from benign MLH1 variants (area under the curve is 0.82 in a receiver-operating characteristic analysis), and therefore hold potential for classification of MLH1 variants of unknown consequence, and hence for LS diagnostics.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Full-length human MLH1 is a 756 residue protein.
source: Full-length human MLH1 is a 756 residue protein which forms two folded units, an N-terminal domain (residues 7–315) and a C-terminal domain (residues 502–756) (Mitchell et al., 2019) separated by a flexible and intrinsically disordered linker (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2019 and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: MLH1 forms two folded units: an N-terminal domain (residues 7–315) and a C-terminal domain (residues 502–756).
source: Full-length human MLH1 is a 756 residue protein which forms two folded units, an N-terminal domain (residues 7–315) and a C-terminal domain (residues 502–756) (Mitchell et al., 2019) separated by a flexible and intrinsically disordered linker (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2019 and structural data.

claim: The N-terminal and C-terminal domains of MLH1 are separated by a flexible and intrinsically disordered linker.
source: Full-length human MLH1 is a 756 residue protein which forms two folded units, an N-terminal domain (residues 7–315) and a C-terminal domain (residues 502–756) (Mitchell et al., 2019) separated by a flexible and intrinsically disordered linker (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2019 and structural knowledge.

claim: The saturation mutagenesis dataset comprises 10,716 different MLH1 variants.
source: Our saturation mutagenesis dataset comprises 19 (amino acids, excluding the wild-type residue) * 564 (residues resolved in the N- and C-terminal structures)=10,716 different MLH1 variants, thus covering 75% of all possible missense variants in MLH1.
evidence: This is a direct calculation based on the number of positions and possible amino acid substitutions.

claim: The saturation mutagenesis dataset covers 75% of all possible missense variants in MLH1.
source: Our saturation mutagenesis dataset comprises 19 (amino acids, excluding the wild-type residue) * 564 (residues resolved in the N- and C-terminal structures)=10,716 different MLH1 variants, thus covering 75% of all possible missense variants in MLH1.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of structurally resolved residues relative to the total protein length.

claim: 34% of the substitutions are expected to change the stability of MLH1 by less than 0.7 kcal/mol.
source: The predictions reveal that 34% of the substitutions are expected to change the stability of MLH1 by less than 0.7 kcal/mol, which is the typical error of the predictions (Guerois et al., 2002) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the computational predictions shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 0.7 kcal/mol is the typical error of the FoldX predictions.
source: The predictions reveal that 34% of the substitutions are expected to change the stability of MLH1 by less than 0.7 kcal/mol, which is the typical error of the predictions (Guerois et al., 2002) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guerois et al., 2002.

claim: 32% of MLH1 substitutions are predicted to cause a substantial destabilization (>2.5 kcal/mol).
source: A comparable fraction (32%) are, however, predicted to cause a substantial destabilization (>2.5 kcal/mol) of the MLH1 protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the computational predictions shown in Figure 1E.

claim: All (likely) benign variants had steady-state levels > 70%.
source: We found that all (likely) benign variants appeared stable and had steady-state levels > 70% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 18 out of 29 pathogenic variants (62%) had steady-state levels < 70%.
source: Conversely, 18 out of the 29 pathogenic variants (62%) had steady-state levels < 70% (Figure 2B), suggesting that protein destabilization is a common feature for more than half of the MLH1 variants linked to LS, and that predictions of stability might be useful for classifying such variants (see below).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Protein destabilization is a common feature for more than half of the MLH1 variants linked to Lynch syndrome.
source: Conversely, 18 out of the 29 pathogenic variants (62%) had steady-state levels < 70% (Figure 2B), suggesting that protein destabilization is a common feature for more than half of the MLH1 variants linked to LS, and that predictions of stability might be useful for classifying such variants (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 62% of pathogenic variants have reduced steady-state levels.

claim: 22 of 23 variants with DME = 3 have steady-state levels > 70%.
source: For example, while 22/23 variants with DME = 3 have steady-state levels > 70%, only five of the 23 variants with DME = 0 have this high amount of protein.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Only 5 of 23 variants with DME = 0 have steady-state levels > 70%.
source: For example, while 22/23 variants with DME = 3 have steady-state levels > 70%, only five of the 23 variants with DME = 0 have this high amount of protein.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: None of the fully functional proteins (DME = 3) are predicted to be destabilized by more than 3 kcal/mol.
source: In particular none of the fully functional proteins (DME = 3) are predicted to be destabilized by more than 3 kcal/mol, whereas 18/23 variants with DME = 0 are predicted to be destabilized by at least this amount.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 18 of 23 variants with DME = 0 are predicted to be destabilized by at least 3 kcal/mol.
source: In particular none of the fully functional proteins (DME = 3) are predicted to be destabilized by more than 3 kcal/mol, whereas 18/23 variants with DME = 0 are predicted to be destabilized by at least this amount.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The unstable and non-functional variants are found throughout both the N- and C-terminal domains of MLH1.
source: The unstable and non-functional variants do not appear structurally clustered to a particular site within the protein, and are found throughout both the N- and C-terminal domains of MLH1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the visualization in Figure 2E.

claim: Affected positions in MLH1 are closer to one another than random pairs in the respective domain.
source: These affected positions are, however, closer to one another than random pairs in the respective domain (average pairwise distances of 17.3 Å vs. 24.1 Å in the N-terminal domain, and 14.7 Å vs. 21.0 Å in the C-terminal domain).
evidence: This is based on structural distance calculations from the crystal structures.

claim: The linker region is depleted in detrimental variants but not in benign variants.
source: In contrast, the linker region is depleted in detrimental variants but not in benign variants, hence functional (Takahashi et al., 2007) and benign (Landrum et al., 2018) variants are found both in structured and unstructured regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Six of the eight selected variants (G67R, R100P, T117M, R265C, K618A, R659P) displayed reduced steady-state levels.
source: Indeed, six of the variants (G67R, R100P, T117M, R265C, K618A, R659P) displayed reduced steady-state levels, while wild type-like levels were observed for two variants (E23D, I219V), in agreement with the fluorescence-based observations (Figure 3AB).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Two variants (E23D, I219V) showed wild type-like steady-state levels.
source: Indeed, six of the variants (G67R, R100P, T117M, R265C, K618A, R659P) displayed reduced steady-state levels, while wild type-like levels were observed for two variants (E23D, I219V), in agreement with the fluorescence-based observations (Figure 3AB).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Variants with reduced steady-state levels were rapidly degraded with half-lives between 3 and 12 hours.
source: This revealed that variants with reduced steady-state levels were indeed rapidly degraded (half-life between 3 and 12 hr), whereas wild-type MLH1 and the other variants appeared stable (estimated half-life >>12 hr) (Figure 3CD).
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Wild-type MLH1 and stable variants have an estimated half-life much greater than 12 hours.
source: This revealed that variants with reduced steady-state levels were indeed rapidly degraded (half-life between 3 and 12 hr), whereas wild-type MLH1 and the other variants appeared stable (estimated half-life >>12 hr) (Figure 3CD).
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Bortezomib treatment significantly increased the steady-state levels of the unstable variants.
source: Treating the cells with the proteasome-inhibitor bortezomib (BZ) significantly increased the steady-state levels of the unstable variants, whereas the levels of the wild-type and stable MLH1 variants were unaffected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Bortezomib treatment did not affect the levels of wild-type and stable MLH1 variants.
source: Treating the cells with the proteasome-inhibitor bortezomib (BZ) significantly increased the steady-state levels of the unstable variants, whereas the levels of the wild-type and stable MLH1 variants were unaffected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Destabilized MLH1 variants appeared more insoluble than stable MLH1 variants.
source: Separating cell lysates into soluble and insoluble fractions by centrifugation revealed that the destabilized MLH1 variants appeared more insoluble than the stable MLH1 variants, and bortezomib treatment mainly caused an increase in the amount of insoluble MLH1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bortezomib treatment mainly caused an increase in the amount of insoluble MLH1.
source: Separating cell lysates into soluble and insoluble fractions by centrifugation revealed that the destabilized MLH1 variants appeared more insoluble than the stable MLH1 variants, and bortezomib treatment mainly caused an increase in the amount of insoluble MLH1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MLH1 associates with PMS2 to form the active MutLα complex.
source: In order to carry out its role in MMR, it is essential that MLH1 associates with PMS2 to form the active MutLα complex (Li and Modrich, 1995; Räschle et al., 2002; Tomer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Modrich, 1995; Räschle et al., 2002; and Tomer et al., 2002.

claim: MLH1 can bind PMS1 to form the MutLβ complex.
source: Additionally, MLH1 can bind the PMS1 protein and form the MutLβ complex, the function of which remains unknown (Cannavo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cannavo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2001; and Wu et al., 2003.

claim: The function of the MutLβ complex remains unknown.
source: Additionally, MLH1 can bind the PMS1 protein and form the MutLβ complex, the function of which remains unknown (Cannavo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the text and supported by citations.

claim: PMS2 is unstable in the absence of MLH1.
source: As typical for 'orphan' proteins lacking their binding partners (Yanagitani et al., 2017; McShane et al., 2016), PMS2 has been found to be unstable in the absence of MLH1 (Hinrichsen et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2015; Mohd et al., 2006; Perera and Bapat, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hinrichsen et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2015; Mohd et al., 2006; and Perera and Bapat, 2008.

claim: In the absence of MLH1, PMS1 and PMS2 are rapidly degraded with half-lives of approximately 3-5 hours.
source: In cells treated with cycloheximide, the absence of MLH1 led to rapid degradation of both PMS1 and PMS2 (t½~3–5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: When wild-type MLH1 was present, PMS1 and PMS2 were dramatically stabilized with half-lives of approximately 12 hours.
source: However, when wild-type MLH1 was present, PMS1 and PMS2 were dramatically stabilized (t½~12 hr) (Figure 4AB).
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Bortezomib treatment led to an increase in the amount of endogenous PMS1 and PMS2.
source: Treating untransfected HCT116 cells with bortezomib led to an increase in the amount of endogenous PMS1 and PMS2, showing that their degradation is proteasome-dependent (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The degradation of PMS1 and PMS2 is proteasome-dependent.
source: Treating untransfected HCT116 cells with bortezomib led to an increase in the amount of endogenous PMS1 and PMS2, showing that their degradation is proteasome-dependent (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteasome inhibition increases PMS1 and PMS2 levels.

claim: MLH1 levels correlated with PMS1 and PMS2 levels.
source: Accordingly, we found that the MLH1 levels correlated with the PMS1 and PMS2 levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Wild-type and stable MLH1 variants (E23D, I219V) were efficiently co-precipitated with YFP-tagged PMS2.
source: We found that the wild-type and stable MLH1 variants (E23D, I219V) were efficiently co-precipitated with the YFP-tagged PMS2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Several unstable MLH1 variants did not display appreciable affinity for PMS2.
source: Several of the unstable MLH1 variants did not display appreciable affinity for PMS2, even after blocking their degradation, suggesting that these MLH1 variants are structurally perturbed or unfolded to an extent that disables complex formation with PMS2.
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Unstable MLH1 variants that do not bind PMS2 are structurally perturbed or unfolded to an extent that disables complex formation with PMS2.
source: Several of the unstable MLH1 variants did not display appreciable affinity for PMS2, even after blocking their degradation, suggesting that these MLH1 variants are structurally perturbed or unfolded to an extent that disables complex formation with PMS2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these variants do not co-precipitate with PMS2 even when degradation is blocked.

claim: The K618A variant displayed a strong interaction with PMS2.
source: Interestingly, the K618A variant displayed a strong interaction with PMS2 (Figure 4H), indicating that this unstable variant retains the ability to bind PMS2, and therefore potentially engage in mismatch repair.
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The K618A variant retains the ability to bind PMS2 and therefore potentially engage in mismatch repair.
source: Interestingly, the K618A variant displayed a strong interaction with PMS2 (Figure 4H), indicating that this unstable variant retains the ability to bind PMS2, and therefore potentially engage in mismatch repair.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that K618A binds PMS2 despite being unstable.

claim: K618 is positioned distally to the PMS2 binding site.
source: We note that this result is supported by the K618A variant's ability to stabilize PMS2 (Figure 4E) and the distal positioning of K618 to the PMS2 binding site (Gueneau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gueneau et al., 2013 and structural knowledge.

claim: Four destabilized MLH1 variants (G67R, R100P, T117M and R265C) displayed strong interaction with HSP70.
source: Interestingly, four of the destabilized MLH1 variants (G67R, R100P, T117M and R265C) displayed a strong interaction with HSP70, up to approximately 7-fold greater compared to wild-type MLH1 (Figure 5AB).
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The interaction of destabilized MLH1 variants with HSP70 was up to approximately 7-fold greater compared to wild-type MLH1.
source: Interestingly, four of the destabilized MLH1 variants (G67R, R100P, T117M and R265C) displayed a strong interaction with HSP70, up to approximately 7-fold greater compared to wild-type MLH1 (Figure 5AB).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HSP90 binds to all tested MLH1 variants, including wild-type.
source: Conversely, in the case of HSP90 we observed binding to all the tested MLH1 variants, including the wild-type (Figure 5CD), suggesting that HSP90 may be involved in the de novo folding of wild-type MLH1 or assembly of MLH1-containing MMR complexes, while HSP70 may be involved in regulation of certain destabilized MLH1 variants, potentially playing a role in their degradation.
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: HSP90 may be involved in the de novo folding of wild-type MLH1 or assembly of MLH1-containing MMR complexes.
source: Conversely, in the case of HSP90 we observed binding to all the tested MLH1 variants, including the wild-type (Figure 5CD), suggesting that HSP90 may be involved in the de novo folding of wild-type MLH1 or assembly of MLH1-containing MMR complexes, while HSP70 may be involved in regulation of certain destabilized MLH1 variants, potentially playing a role in their degradation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that HSP90 binds all variants including wild-type.

claim: HSP70 may be involved in regulation of certain destabilized MLH1 variants, potentially playing a role in their degradation.
source: Conversely, in the case of HSP90 we observed binding to all the tested MLH1 variants, including the wild-type (Figure 5CD), suggesting that HSP90 may be involved in the de novo folding of wild-type MLH1 or assembly of MLH1-containing MMR complexes, while HSP70 may be involved in regulation of certain destabilized MLH1 variants, potentially playing a role in their degradation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the selective binding of HSP70 to destabilized variants.

claim: HSP70 inhibition increased the levels of three variants (G67R, R100P, T117M).
source: The levels of three variants (G67R, R100P, T117M) were, however, increased (Figure 5EF), and all three were also found to bind HSP70 (Figure 5A) and had the lowest steady-state levels of the eight tested variants prior to HSP70 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The three variants whose levels increased upon HSP70 inhibition (G67R, R100P, T117M) also bound HSP70 and had the lowest steady-state levels.
source: The levels of three variants (G67R, R100P, T117M) were, however, increased (Figure 5EF), and all three were also found to bind HSP70 (Figure 5A) and had the lowest steady-state levels of the eight tested variants prior to HSP70 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 5A, 5E-F, and 3B.

claim: HSP70 actively partakes in detecting and/or directing certain destabilized MLH1 variants for degradation.
source: Together, these results suggest that HSP70 actively partakes in detecting and/or directing certain destabilized MLH1 variants for degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HSP70 inhibition increases levels of certain destabilized variants that also bind HSP70.

claim: HSP90 inhibition did not affect MLH1 protein levels for any of the tested variants.
source: We did not observe any effect of HSP90 inhibition on the MLH1 protein levels for any of the tested variants (Figure 5GH).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: FoldX provides an orthogonal structure-based and sequence-conservation-independent prediction of whether a mutation is likely to be pathogenic.
source: In comparison with the sequence-based tools (e.g. PolyPhen2, PROVEAN and REVEL) that are currently employed in the clinic (Adzhubei et al., 2010; Choi and Chan, 2015), the FoldX energy predictions provide an orthogonal structure-based and sequence-conservation-independent prediction of whether a mutation is likely to be pathogenic.
evidence: This is based on the nature of the FoldX method which uses structural information rather than sequence conservation.

claim: FoldX was not trained on whether mutations were benign or pathogenic, but solely on biophysical stability measurements.
source: Unlike most variant consequence predictors, FoldX was not trained on whether mutations were benign or pathogenic, but solely on biophysical stability measurements (Guerois et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guerois et al., 2002 describing the FoldX method.

claim: Training FoldX solely on biophysical measurements considerably reduces the risk of overfitting to known pathogenic variants.
source: This considerably reduces the risk of overfitting to known pathogenic variants.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that FoldX was not trained on pathogenicity data.

claim: FoldX predictions enable insights into why a particular mutation is problematic due to the mechanistic link to protein stability.
source: More importantly, because of the mechanistic link to protein stability, FoldX predictions enable insights into why a particular mutation is problematic (Kiel and Serrano, 2014; Kiel et al., 2016; Pey et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2017; Stein et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating the utility of stability predictions.

claim: MLH1 variants reported at high frequency in gnomAD all displayed low ΔΔG values.
source: Gratifyingly, this revealed that those variants reported to occur at a high frequency in the population all displayed low ΔΔG values (Figure 6A), suggesting that these MLH1 proteins are stable.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The most common MLH1 alleles reported in gnomAD appeared functional (high DME scores).
source: Accordingly, with only a few exceptions, the most common MLH1 alleles reported in gnomAD also appeared functional (high DME scores) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All benign MLH1 variants in the dataset appeared structurally stable.
source: This revealed that the benign MLH1 variants all appeared structurally stable, while many pathogenic variants appeared destabilized (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 15 of 28 pathogenic variants (54%) have ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol.
source: For example, in our dataset 15 of the 28 pathogenic variants (54%) for which we could calculate a stability change have ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol and 20 (71%) have ΔΔG > 2 kcal/mol, whereas none of the 11 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on the computational predictions for the variants in the study.

claim: 20 of 28 pathogenic variants (71%) have ΔΔG > 2 kcal/mol.
source: For example, in our dataset 15 of the 28 pathogenic variants (54%) for which we could calculate a stability change have ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol and 20 (71%) have ΔΔG > 2 kcal/mol, whereas none of the 11 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on the computational predictions for the variants in the study.

claim: None of the 11 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
source: For example, in our dataset 15 of the 28 pathogenic variants (54%) for which we could calculate a stability change have ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol and 20 (71%) have ΔΔG > 2 kcal/mol, whereas none of the 11 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on the computational predictions for the variants in the study.

claim: 55 of 95 (57%) pathogenic variants in ClinVar have ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol.
source: Applying this calculation to all MLH1 missense variants in ClinVar revealed similar trends, with 55/95 (57%) of the pathogenic variants having ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol, while only 2/21 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on computational predictions applied to all ClinVar variants.

claim: Only 2 of 21 benign variants in ClinVar have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
source: Applying this calculation to all MLH1 missense variants in ClinVar revealed similar trends, with 55/95 (57%) of the pathogenic variants having ΔΔG > 3 kcal/mol, while only 2/21 benign variants have ΔΔG > 1.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on computational predictions applied to all ClinVar variants.

claim: The logistic regression model combining FoldX ΔΔG and evolutionary sequence energies correctly classified 99 of 116 (85%) ClinVar missense variants.
source: In a jackknife test (to avoid overfitting) we found that 99 of 116 (85%) ClinVar (Landrum et al., 2018) missense variants were classified correctly by the regression model (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the jackknife analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The logistic regression model performs best with AUC of 0.90 ± 0.03.
source: The results show that although all predictors perform fairly well, the logistic regression model performs best (AUC: 0.90 ± 0.03), and evolutionary sequence energies alone (AUC: 0.88 ± 0.03) are slightly better at distinguishing disease-linked missense variants from harmless variants than REVEL (AUC: 0.83 ± 0.03), PolyPhen2 (AUC: 0.84 ± 0.03) and PROVEAN (AUC: 0.76 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Evolutionary sequence energies alone have AUC of 0.88 ± 0.03.
source: The results show that although all predictors perform fairly well, the logistic regression model performs best (AUC: 0.90 ± 0.03), and evolutionary sequence energies alone (AUC: 0.88 ± 0.03) are slightly better at distinguishing disease-linked missense variants from harmless variants than REVEL (AUC: 0.83 ± 0.03), PolyPhen2 (AUC: 0.84 ± 0.03) and PROVEAN (AUC: 0.76 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: REVEL has AUC of 0.83 ± 0.03 for distinguishing pathogenic from benign MLH1 variants.
source: The results show that although all predictors perform fairly well, the logistic regression model performs best (AUC: 0.90 ± 0.03), and evolutionary sequence energies alone (AUC: 0.88 ± 0.03) are slightly better at distinguishing disease-linked missense variants from harmless variants than REVEL (AUC: 0.83 ± 0.03), PolyPhen2 (AUC: 0.84 ± 0.03) and PROVEAN (AUC: 0.76 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PolyPhen2 has AUC of 0.84 ± 0.03 for distinguishing pathogenic from benign MLH1 variants.
source: The results show that although all predictors perform fairly well, the logistic regression model performs best (AUC: 0.90 ± 0.03), and evolutionary sequence energies alone (AUC: 0.88 ± 0.03) are slightly better at distinguishing disease-linked missense variants from harmless variants than REVEL (AUC: 0.83 ± 0.03), PolyPhen2 (AUC: 0.84 ± 0.03) and PROVEAN (AUC: 0.76 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PROVEAN has AUC of 0.76 ± 0.04 for distinguishing pathogenic from benign MLH1 variants.
source: The results show that although all predictors perform fairly well, the logistic regression model performs best (AUC: 0.90 ± 0.03), and evolutionary sequence energies alone (AUC: 0.88 ± 0.03) are slightly better at distinguishing disease-linked missense variants from harmless variants than REVEL (AUC: 0.83 ± 0.03), PolyPhen2 (AUC: 0.84 ± 0.03) and PROVEAN (AUC: 0.76 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Structure-based ΔΔG calculations show similar performance to sequence-based predictors (AUC: 0.82 ± 0.04).
source: Structure-based ΔΔG calculations show similar performance to these sequence-based predictors (AUC: 0.82 ± 0.04), but, as the shape of the ROC curve illustrates, are particularly informative in the region of high specificity.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 19 of 116 (16%) ClinVar variants may affect splicing.
source: Using SpliceAI (Jaganathan et al., 2019) we predicted that 19/116 (16%) of the ClinVar variants may affect splicing.
evidence: This is based on SpliceAI predictions shown in Figure 6G.

claim: All 19 variants predicted to affect splicing are pathogenic variants; no benign variants were predicted to affect splicing.
source: All 19 are pathogenic variants; no benign variants were predicted to affect splicing.
evidence: This is based on SpliceAI predictions shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 4 of 7 erroneously classified variants may affect splicing rather than protein function.
source: Interestingly, 4 of these variants have scores in our regression model that suggest them to be non-detrimental, and thus predicted not to affect protein function or stability (Figure 6G). Hence, more than half (4/7) of these erroneously classified variants may affect splicing rather that protein function, a substantially higher fraction than the 17% (15/88) that are predicted to affect splicing among those variants that are correctly classified by our regression model integrating ΔΔG and evolutionary sequence energies.
evidence: This is based on the integration of SpliceAI predictions with the regression model results shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Missense variants in MLH1 are a leading cause of Lynch syndrome.
source: Missense variants in the MLH1 gene are a leading cause of Lynch syndrome (LS) and colorectal cancer (Peltomäki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peltomäki, 2016.

claim: Germline mutations that cause structural destabilization and subsequent protein misfolding are the cause of several diseases.
source: In recent years, germline mutations that cause structural destabilization and subsequent protein misfolding have surfaced as the cause of several diseases, including cystic fibrosis (Ahner et al., 2007), phenylketonuria (Pey et al., 2007; Scheller et al., 2019), early onset Parkinson's disease (Mathiassen et al., 2015; Olzmann et al., 2004) and MSH2-linked LS (Arlow et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on different diseases.

claim: Previous studies have shown some MLH1 variants to be destabilized.
source: Although previous studies have shown some MLH1 variants to be destabilized (Takahashi et al., 2007; Perera and Bapat, 2008), this has not been systematically addressed and the contribution of MLH1 protein stability for LS remains to be resolved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2007 and Perera and Bapat, 2008.

claim: The contribution of MLH1 protein stability for Lynch syndrome has not been systematically addressed.
source: Although previous studies have shown some MLH1 variants to be destabilized (Takahashi et al., 2007; Perera and Bapat, 2008), this has not been systematically addressed and the contribution of MLH1 protein stability for LS remains to be resolved.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the text.

claim: Single amino acid changes in MLH1 are sufficient to cause degradation.
source: Our observation that single amino acid changes in MLH1 are sufficient to cause degradation is similar to results from multiple other proteins including recent deep mutational scans on PTEN and TPMT (Matreyek et al., 2018), our previous results on MSH2 in human cells (Nielsen et al., 2017), and earlier observations on Lynch syndrome MSH2 variants in yeast (Gammie et al., 2007; Arlow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in this study and citations to similar findings in other proteins.

claim: A relatively mild destabilization of approximately 3 kcal/mol is sufficient to trigger MLH1 degradation.
source: Our structural stability calculations predict that a relatively mild destabilization of just a few (~3) kcal/mol is sufficient to trigger MLH1 degradation, an observation in line with previous studies on other proteins (Bullock et al., 2000; Nielsen et al., 2017; DDD Study et al., 2017; Scheller et al., 2019; Jepsen et al., 2019; Caswell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between predicted ΔΔG and measured degradation, and citations to similar findings in other proteins.

claim: Wild-type MLH1 is perhaps only marginally stable.
source: Although we show that wild-type MLH1 is perhaps only marginally stable, we propose that these effects of slightly destabilizing amino acid substitutions could be the result of local unfolding events rather than global unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by the thermal stability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of slightly destabilizing amino acid substitutions could be the result of local unfolding events rather than global unfolding.
source: Although we show that wild-type MLH1 is perhaps only marginally stable, we propose that these effects of slightly destabilizing amino acid substitutions could be the result of local unfolding events rather than global unfolding.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that mild destabilization triggers degradation.

claim: The protein quality control system is tightly tuned to detect increased amounts of minor or transient structural defects.
source: Accordingly, it appears that the PQC system is tightly tuned to detect increased amounts of minor or transient structural defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mild destabilization is sufficient to trigger degradation.

claim: The protein quality control system preferably targets folding intermediates.
source: This is supported by observations on MSH2 showing that in some cases the destabilized variants are even functional when degradation is blocked (Arlow et al., 2013), and results showing that the PQC system preferably targets folding intermediates (Bershtein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arlow et al., 2013 and Bershtein et al., 2013.

claim: In some cases, destabilized MSH2 variants are functional when degradation is blocked.
source: This is supported by observations on MSH2 showing that in some cases the destabilized variants are even functional when degradation is blocked (Arlow et al., 2013), and results showing that the PQC system preferably targets folding intermediates (Bershtein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arlow et al., 2013.

claim: Predictions of changes to global folding stability are effective in distinguishing variants that are stable in the cell from those that are more rapidly degraded.
source: As a result, it is surprising that predictions of changes to the global folding stability (using the fully unfolded state as a reference) are so effective in distinguishing variants that are stable in the cell from those that are more rapidly degraded.
evidence: This is based on the correlation between predicted ΔΔG and measured cellular stability shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Improved understanding of the biophysical basis for cellular quality control might lead to even better predictions of cellular abundance.
source: These observations also suggest that improved understanding of the biophysical basis for cellular quality control might lead to even better predictions of cellular abundance.
evidence: This is speculated based on the current limitations of the predictions.

claim: Multiple disease-linked MLH1 variants will display reduced cellular levels.
source: Nevertheless, since the predicted protein stabilities can, to a large extent, discriminate between pathogenic and benign variants, we expect that multiple disease-linked MLH1 variants will indeed display reduced cellular levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between predicted stability and pathogenicity.

claim: Structural destabilization appears to be a common consequence of many disease-linked MLH1 missense variants.
source: Similar to our previous observations for MSH2 (Nielsen et al., 2017), these results indicate that structural destabilization appears to be a common consequence of many disease-linked MLH1 missense variants.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that 62% of pathogenic variants have reduced steady-state levels.

claim: The loss-of-function phenotype in many cases can be explained by structural destabilization and subsequent degradation.
source: Supported by earlier functional studies (Takahashi et al., 2007), we suggest that the loss-of-function phenotype in many cases can be explained by structural destabilization and subsequent degradation.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between stability, cellular levels, and function, along with citation to Takahashi et al., 2007.

claim: 20 out of 31 variants with DME = 0 or DME = 1 have steady-state levels less than 70% of wildtype MLH1.
source: Indeed, 20 out of the 31 variants with DME = 0 or DME = 1 have steady-state levels less than 70% of wildtype MLH1.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: Variants can affect function without modifying stability, for example by changing binding interfaces or active sites.
source: Our data also include examples of loss-of-function variants with high steady-state levels, which is expected, as variants can affect function without modifying stability, for example, by changing binding interfaces or active sites (Gueneau et al., 2013), and these would therefore be interesting to analyze biochemically in more detail.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of protein function and supported by citation to Gueneau et al., 2013.

claim: According to ClinVar, 711 out of 851 (~84%) reported MLH1 missense variants are assigned as variants of uncertain significance.
source: This is particularly relevant for LS, where according to the ClinVar database (Landrum et al., 2018) 711 out of 851 (~84%) reported MLH1 missense variants are assigned as so-called variants of uncertain significance (VUS) (Manolio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on data from the ClinVar database cited as Landrum et al., 2018.

claim: The E23D variant may be pathogenic despite not being destabilized, as it may affect function.
source: Of note, the fact that we did not observe the E23D VUS as destabilized does not preclude this variant from being pathogenic, since it may affect function without being structurally perturbed.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that E23D is not destabilized but has a high evolutionary sequence energy.

claim: The K618A variant, albeit being unstable, is still able to associate with PMS2 and may therefore be functional but untimely degraded.
source: Our results for the K618A VUS suggest that this variant, albeit being unstable, is still able to associate with PMS2 and may therefore be functional, but untimely degraded.
evidence: This is based on the observation that K618A binds PMS2 despite being unstable (Figure 4H).

claim: Several VUS variants (G54E, G244V, and L676R) hold characteristics indicating they are likely pathogenic.
source: Of the 69 MLH1 variants that we analyzed, 30 have status as VUSs. Of these, our analysis identified several (e.g. G54E, G244V, and L676R) that hold characteristics indicating that they are likely pathogenic: steady-state levels below 50% of WT, high ΔΔG and low functionality score in vivo (Takahashi et al., 2007) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on the combination of low steady-state levels, high ΔΔG, and low DME scores shown in Table 1.

claim: In a cellular context, it is unlikely that any of the variants are fully unfolded; instead, local elements likely unfold.
source: As described above, it is important to note that the stability predictions report on the global stability of the protein, while in a cellular context it is unlikely that any of the variants are fully unfolded. Instead, it is likely that local elements unfold (Stein et al., 2019), and although refolding may occur, the locally unfolded state allows chaperones and other protein quality control components to associate and target the protein for proteasomal degradation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that mild destabilization triggers degradation, and supported by citation to Stein et al., 2019.

claim: The locally unfolded state allows chaperones and other protein quality control components to associate and target the protein for proteasomal degradation.
source: Instead, it is likely that local elements unfold (Stein et al., 2019), and although refolding may occur, the locally unfolded state allows chaperones and other protein quality control components to associate and target the protein for proteasomal degradation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of protein quality control mechanisms and supported by citation to Stein et al., 2019.

claim: A better understanding of the importance of local unfolding events for cellular stability is an important area for further research.
source: A better understanding of the importance of local unfolding events for cellular stability is an important area for further research.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future research.

claim: The stability calculations can identify approximately 60% of pathogenic variants at very high specificity.
source: This observation is also supported by our ROC analysis (Figure 6D), which demonstrates that the stability calculations can identify ~60% of the pathogenic variants at very high specificity (few false positives) exactly because these are the variants that appear to cause disease via this mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Approximately 60% of disease-causing variants in PTEN were caused by destabilization and resulting drop in cellular abundance.
source: Incidentally, we note that by analyzing both calculations and multiplexed assays of variant effects, we recently found that ~60% of disease-causing variants in the protein PTEN were caused by destabilization and a resulting drop in cellular abundance (Jepsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jepsen et al., 2019.

claim: Stability prediction is very useful for accurate identification of many pathogenic variants, but may have lower overall sensitivity.
source: On the other hand, while stability prediction is very useful for accurate identification of many pathogenic variants, it may have lower overall sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the ROC analysis showing high specificity but not perfect sensitivity.

claim: Destabilized variants are likely pathogenic, while a variant being stable does not necessarily imply it being functional.
source: We speculate that this is due to stability being a necessary, but not sufficient criterion. Thus, destabilized variants are likely pathogenic, while a variant being stable does not necessary imply it being functional.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that some stable variants are still pathogenic.

claim: Degradation signals (degrons) are buried within the native structure of most globular proteins.
source: Moreover, our findings are consistent with recent developments in the field, showing that degradation signals, so-called degrons, are buried within the native structure of most globular proteins.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field of protein quality control.

claim: Upon exposure when the protein structure is destabilized, degrons are recognized by chaperones and other protein quality control components.
source: Upon exposure when the protein structure is destabilized, the degrons are recognized by chaperones and other protein quality control components, which in turn guide the target protein for degradation (Enam et al., 2018; Geffen et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2013; Maurer et al., 2016; Ravid and Hochstrasser, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on protein quality control.

claim: The degradation of a protein depends on both the structural destabilization (ΔΔG) and the exposed degrons.
source: Thus, ultimately the degradation of a protein will depend on both the structural destabilization (ΔΔG) as well as the exposed degrons, and how efficiently these are recognized by the degradation machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the understanding of protein quality control mechanisms.

claim: Biophysical calculations are able to predict the structural destabilization (ΔΔG).
source: The results presented here suggest that biophysical calculations are able to predict the structural destabilization (ΔΔG), however, since the nature of protein quality control degrons is still largely undefined (Geffen et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2016; Rosenbaum et al., 2011; van der Lee et al., 2014), in silico prediction of these is currently not possible.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between predicted ΔΔG and measured cellular stability.

claim: The nature of protein quality control degrons is still largely undefined.
source: The results presented here suggest that biophysical calculations are able to predict the structural destabilization (ΔΔG), however, since the nature of protein quality control degrons is still largely undefined (Geffen et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2016; Rosenbaum et al., 2011; van der Lee et al., 2014), in silico prediction of these is currently not possible.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on protein quality control.

claim: In silico prediction of protein quality control degrons is currently not possible.
source: The results presented here suggest that biophysical calculations are able to predict the structural destabilization (ΔΔG), however, since the nature of protein quality control degrons is still largely undefined (Geffen et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2016; Rosenbaum et al., 2011; van der Lee et al., 2014), in silico prediction of these is currently not possible.
evidence: This is stated explicitly based on the current state of knowledge.

claim: Missense mutations can cause destabilization of MLH1, leading to exposure of degrons which trigger HSP70-assisted proteasomal degradation.
source: In conclusion, our results support a model (Figure 7) where missense mutations can cause destabilization of the MLH1 protein, leading to exposure of degrons which, in turn, trigger HSP70-assisted proteasomal degradation, causing disruption of the MMR pathway and ultimately leading to an increased cumulative lifetime risk of cancer development in LS patients.
evidence: This is the overall model supported by all the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: HSP70-assisted proteasomal degradation of MLH1 causes disruption of the MMR pathway.
source: In conclusion, our results support a model (Figure 7) where missense mutations can cause destabilization of the MLH1 protein, leading to exposure of degrons which, in turn, trigger HSP70-assisted proteasomal degradation, causing disruption of the MMR pathway and ultimately leading to an increased cumulative lifetime risk of cancer development in LS patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MLH1 degradation leads to loss of MMR function.

claim: Disruption of the MMR pathway ultimately leads to an increased cumulative lifetime risk of cancer development in Lynch syndrome patients.
source: In conclusion, our results support a model (Figure 7) where missense mutations can cause destabilization of the MLH1 protein, leading to exposure of degrons which, in turn, trigger HSP70-assisted proteasomal degradation, causing disruption of the MMR pathway and ultimately leading to an increased cumulative lifetime risk of cancer development in LS patients.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that MMR deficiency leads to cancer.

claim: The findings open up possibilities for new therapeutic approaches, including inhibiting PQC-mediated clearance of marginally stable MLH1 variants or using small molecule stabilizers of MLH1.
source: Potentially, this opens up for new therapeutic approaches, including inhibiting the PQC-mediated clearance of marginally stable MLH1 variants, or small molecule stabilizers of MLH1.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential therapeutic application of the findings.
